title: Public-health governance is increasingly a signal-filtering and data-quality system, not only a count of confirmed disease events
source_unit: World Health Organization, Weekly Epidemiological Record, Volume 101 Issue 38, epidemiological week 38 of 2026
geography: Global public-health surveillance, with regional respiratory-virus, cholera, meningitis, plague, and event-based surveillance reporting

denominator.unit: raw signals screened by WHO Public Health Intelligence activities

signals_categorized.unit: signals categorized for detailed assessment and action

unique_signals.unit: unique signals after removing repeated or duplicate signals

signals_escalated.unit: categorized signals escalated for operational attention

public_outputs.unit: Rapid Risk Assessment published during the reporting week

observations.method: WHO weekly summary of digital event-based surveillance, with explicit funnel definitions for screened, categorized, unique, and escalated signals.
observations.uncertainty: Signal counts measure surveillance workflow, not disease incidence or the probability that an escalated signal becomes an outbreak; thresholds, duplication, language, source access, and analyst capacity shape the funnel.
observations.subgroup: Public-health intelligence teams, ministries, laboratories, communities generating or exposed to signals, and populations affected by later assessment and response decisions.
observations.counterinterpretation: A large screened-to-escalated reduction can reflect effective triage, but it can also reflect blind spots, low-quality reporting, or thresholds that delay attention to weak or marginalized signals.

regional_variation.value: positivity above 30% in some countries or zones in Western Africa and parts of Asia and Oceania

observations.method: WHO Global Influenza Surveillance and Response System summary of reported specimens and positivity by region.
observations.uncertainty: Positivity depends on who is tested, specimen volume, reporting coverage, timing, and surveillance-system composition; it is not a population infection prevalence estimate.
observations.subgroup: People tested through national respiratory-virus surveillance, health systems, and regions with different testing intensity and pathogen circulation.
observations.counterinterpretation: Low global or stable positivity can coexist with localized surges, under-testing, delayed reporting, or severe outcomes among vulnerable groups.

observations.period: 2025; enhanced meningitis surveillance in the African meningitis belt

denominator.unit: countries in the enhanced meningitis surveillance network

suspected_cases.unit: suspected meningitis cases reported over the full year

deaths.unit: reported meningitis deaths over the full year

case_fatality_rate.unit: reported case-fatality rate among reported suspected cases

observations.method: WHO synthesis of country and laboratory surveillance data for 2025, with like-for-like comparisons restricted to countries reporting in both 2024 and 2025.
observations.uncertainty: Non-reporting by Ethiopia and Uganda, uneven laboratory participation, suspected rather than confirmed cases, and changing reporting pools limit trend interpretation; absent reporting is not absence of disease.
observations.subgroup: People in the African meningitis-belt surveillance network, district health systems, laboratories, vaccine programs, and communities exposed to epidemic risk or long-term sequelae.
observations.counterinterpretation: Lower reported cases can reflect real progress, surveillance changes, vaccination, missing data, or altered laboratory participation; the crude decline cannot be read as an equivalent decline in underlying burden.

denominator.unit: WHO public-health surveillance and prevention system frame

surveillance_expansion.value: enhanced meningitis surveillance expanded from 8 countries in 2003 to 26 in 2025

serogroup_a_change.value: more than 99% reduction in confirmed serogroup A disease in vaccinated populations, with no confirmed case reported since 2017 in countries introducing MenACV

men5cv_reach.value: 3,288,785 people reached by reactive Men5CV campaigns in Chad, Niger, and Nigeria

system_condition.value: consistent reporting, laboratory surveillance, integrated vaccination, clinical access, national plans, and predictable financing remain necessary

observations.method: WHO longitudinal program and surveillance synthesis combining network expansion, vaccination, laboratory, reporting, and implementation information.
observations.uncertainty: The record describes program and surveillance progress but does not isolate causal vaccine effects across all settings or establish equal access, durability, or sequelae care.
observations.subgroup: Children, adolescents, adults, vaccinated and unvaccinated communities, laboratories, district health systems, and people living with meningitis-related disability.
observations.counterinterpretation: Successful prevention in one serogroup or population can coexist with other serogroups, reporting gaps, access inequality, and persistent long-term disability among survivors.

related_sources.claim: WHO health-emergency information and risk-assessment context for event-based surveillance and early warning.
WHO Defeating Meningitis by 2030 road-map context for surveillance, vaccination, care, and prevention.

boundary: This record adds a public-health sensing and surveillance-infrastructure signal linking raw signals, triage, escalation, respiratory-virus monitoring, reporting quality, laboratory participation, vaccination, and preparedness. It is a WHO weekly surveillance publication, not a complete event census, population infection prevalence estimate, causal vaccine evaluation, respondent-level dataset, or proof that low reported signals mean low underlying risk.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official WHO Weekly Epidemiological Record page was reviewed for the week-38 event-based surveillance funnel, week-37 respiratory-virus summary, 2025 meningitis surveillance network and reporting caveats, vaccination program measures, and the distinction between missing data and no disease.
